notes:
Need to search first.I've put together verse notes for 1 Kings 4, but they cover less than you asked for. The research tool hit its usage limit partway through, so I only got through enduringword.com and the older commentaries collected on biblehub, studylight, blueletterbible and preceptaustin. I didn't reach netbible, bibleodyssey, any Catholic or Orthodox site, or anything on prosperity or word-of-faith teaching, so those sections are left out. Verses 10, 12–14 and 16–18 are left out too, because nothing I read commented on them.

For the same reason, I only name a commentator's church tradition when the page itself gave it. StudyLight labels Adam Clarke and Joseph Benson as "Wesleyan/Methodist", so those two stand for the Methodist side.

---

**v. 1** – Gill: "over all Israel" is set against David, who first ruled only Judah, and against the kings after the split. He also thinks it may mean Solomon reigned with the whole people's consent because of the wisdom shown in ch. 3. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html
– Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the chapter describes the kingdom at its height, in the more flourishing later years of Solomon's reign. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ki/1Ki_004.cfm
– Guzik: the list of officials shows Solomon's wisdom too. A wise leader delegates and chooses, trains and oversees the right people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/
– Constable: delegating is a sign of wisdom in someone who has more to do than one person can manage. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-4.html

**v. 2** – Constable and Preceptaustin: Azariah was probably Zadok's grandson, the son of Ahimaaz (1 Chr 6:8–9). Constable notes "the priest" is a usual title for the high priest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-1.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-4-commentary
– **Interpretations differ on the word *kohen*.**
  - Barnes says that with the article it can only mean "the high priest." Azariah is listed first because he held that office. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-2.htm
  - Ellicott also takes it as "priest," given to Azariah ahead of time, since v. 4 still names Zadok and Abiathar. In his view, priestly and princely roles overlapped in this period. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/4.htm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown reads "prince" instead, making Azariah a prime minister. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ki/1Ki_004.cfm
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary calls the office secular, not priestly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-kings-4.html
  - Benson gives both options: a second priest serving the king, or the chief minister of state. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-2.htm

**v. 3** – Gill: Shisha is the same man as Sheva, David's scribe (2 Sam 20:25). His two sons were probably kept on because Solomon had more state business. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html
– Guzik, quoting Wiseman: Jehoshaphat, who had also served David, was more a chief of protocol than a keeper of records, almost a Secretary of State. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/

**v. 4** – Why is Abiathar listed when Solomon had banished him (2:26)?
  - Guzik, quoting Dilday: Solomon could take away his duties but not his title or dignity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/
  - Ellicott: the priesthood was for life, so Abiathar was still priest in theory, much as Annas is called high priest in the Gospels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/4.htm
  - Gill: he kept the name after being removed. Gill cites Jewish views that he may have stood in for Zadok when needed, and Kimchi, who thought a different Abiathar was meant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html
  - Preceptaustin: Azariah was the one actually serving. Zadok and Abiathar were probably listed to honour their service under David. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-4-commentary

**v. 5** – **Which Nathan?**
  - Gill takes him to be Nathan the prophet, rewarded for helping Solomon to the throne. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-5.html
  - Ellicott, and Keil & Delitzsch, say it was David's son Nathan, which would make Azariah and Zabud Solomon's nephews. Their reasons: 2 Sam 8:18 gives the title *kohen* to "sons of David", and this book always calls the prophet "Nathan the prophet." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/4.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-5.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says it can't be settled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-5.htm
– Keil & Delitzsch: Luther and many others translated "son of Nathan the priest." K&D reject this and read *kohen* together with "king's friend," meaning a trusted privy councillor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-5.htm
– Rawlinson, cited in the Pulpit Commentary: "king's friend" seems to have been a recognised office by now, the role Hushai held under David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-5.htm
– Gill: Azariah was over the twelve officers in v. 7. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-5.html

**v. 6** – Gill: Adoniram held the same job under David (2 Sam 20:24). The Targum makes him head of those who collected tribute. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html

**v. 7** – Gill: the twelve were matched to the twelve months, not the twelve tribes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html
– Guzik:
  - The districts followed geography more than tribe, which shows a creative leader.
  - Taxes were paid in grain and livestock.
  - One month a year each meant the burden wasn't oppressive.
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/
– Constable: the plan seems meant to move Israel from tribal independence toward a central government, though the borders were close to the old tribal lines. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-4.html

**v. 8** – Gill: several men are named only by their fathers' names, because the fathers were well known. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html

**v. 9** – Gill: Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan are all in Dan (Josh 19:41). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html

**vv. 11, 15** – Constable: two of the governors were Solomon's sons-in-law. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-4.html

**v. 19** – The "one governor in the land": readings differ.
  - Gill reports that some thought it meant Azariah (v. 5) over all the rest. He prefers the Jewish view of an extra officer for the leap-year 13th month. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html
  - Guzik, quoting Wiseman: it means one official for Judah, the home territory, which was kept apart from the twelve districts. Some say Judah wasn't taxed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/
  - Ellicott doubts Judah was left out of the tax system. He suggests Azariah may have governed it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/4.htm

**v. 20** – Henry, the Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott: the promise to Abraham of descendants "as the sand" (Gen 22:17) is fulfilled here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-20.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-20.htm
– **"Eating, drinking and rejoicing": praise or warning?**
  - Henry treats it as good. Solomon taught the people to enjoy what they had with sober cheerfulness, not to hoard it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-20.html
  - Gill and Trapp read it as a picture of the joy believers have in Christ's kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-20.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/1ki-4.cfm
  - The two Methodists are much sharper. Clarke says the people were comfortable, merry "and very corrupt," and that the plenty ruined their morals. Benson recalls Deut 32:15, where Jeshurun grew fat and kicked, and asks who can bear constant prosperity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-20.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-20.htm
  - Coffman: the people were living off other nations' tribute, and rebelled once the cost fell on them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-20.html
– Preceptaustin: Judah and Israel are named separately, possibly hinting at the split in ch. 11. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-4-commentary

**v. 21** – Guzik: David won this peace, and Solomon enjoyed it. The neighbouring states were also weak at the time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/
– Barnes and Ellicott: this was a group of small tributary kingdoms, not a unified state. Ellicott says it was held together more by wealth, policy and Solomon's personal standing than by armies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-21.htm
– Henry and Gill: v. 21 fits Psalm 72 and looks ahead to Christ's wider kingdom. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_004.cfm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-21.html
– **Was the promise to Abraham fulfilled?**
  - Benson and Poole say yes: God's promise of land to the Euphrates came true here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-21.htm
  - Constable says Solomon ruled the promised area but didn't fully fulfil the promise, since the land wasn't within Israel's borders. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-21.html
  - MacArthur, quoted on Preceptaustin, says Solomon's reign was not the fulfilment, partly because Israel only lived "from Dan to Beersheba." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-4-commentary

**vv. 22–23** – Guzik:
  - The food fed the whole court. Some estimate 15,000–36,000 people a day.
  - A cor was about 220 litres.
  - The point is the kingdom's prosperity, not luxury.
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/
– Gill puts the cor at about 75 wine gallons. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html

**v. 24** – Gill: Solomon's peace on every side makes him a type of Christ, the Prince of Peace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html
– Constable: Tiphsah stood on the Euphrates. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-4.html

**v. 25** – Guzik: "vine and fig tree" was a common saying for peace and safety from enemies inside and out (Mic 4:4; Zech 3:10). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/
– Clarke: people no longer had to crowd into walled cities. They spread out and ate what they had grown. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-25.html
– Henry: Solomon didn't seize people's property (contrast 1 Sam 8:14). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-25.html
– Gill and Keil & Delitzsch: the prophets use this phrase for the Messiah's age. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-25.htm
– Maclaren, quoted on the same page: a picture of quiet, contented country life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-25.htm

**v. 26** – **4,000 or 40,000?**
  - Barnes, Clarke, Constable and the Pulpit Commentary think "40,000" is a copying error for 2 Chr 9:25's 4,000. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-26.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-26.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/9-25.html
  - Gill and Poole try to reconcile the two, for example 40,000 stalls in 4,000 stables. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-26.htm
  - Coffman thinks 40,000 is just as likely correct. Chuck Smith points to stables found by archaeologists. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-26.html
  - Preceptaustin quotes Mattoon on how Hebrew number-letters could be miscopied. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-4-commentary
– Guzik: this broke Deut 17:16, "he shall not multiply horses." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/
– Poole: possibly God gave a special permission, though none is recorded. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-26.htm

**v. 27** – Gill: the food also served visitors from abroad who came to see the court. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html

**v. 28** – Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik, preached on "every man according to his charge." Every believer has a task in Christ's kingdom and should give in proportion to his means. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/

**v. 29** – Gill: Solomon's wisdom came as God's gift, not from natural talent or effort (Jas 1:5). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html
– Henry on "largeness of heart": a wide grasp of knowledge, or boldness, or generosity in sharing what he knew. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/4-29.html
– Poole: it means a vast understanding, like sand, huge yet made of tiny grains. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-29.htm
– Guzik: Solomon later stopped using this wisdom (11:1–11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/

**v. 30** – Gill: the "men of the East" were Arabians and Persians, known for astronomy and fortune-telling. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html

**v. 31** – Guzik:
  - Ethan wrote Psalm 89 and Heman wrote Psalm 88.
  - Solomon's fame fits the blessings promised to an obedient Israel in Deut 28.
  - Those blessings came more for David's sake than Solomon's.
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/

**v. 32** – Gill: the 3,000 proverbs were spoken and later lost. The inspired book of Proverbs survived, and the Song of Songs is the finest of his songs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html
– Guzik: Solomon wrote many songs but few psalms, which he links to a weaker walk with God than David's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/

**v. 33** – Guzik, quoting Dilday: cedar ranked highest among plants and hyssop lowest, so the phrase covers everything. Quoting Wiseman: kings of the time boasted of their zoos and botanical gardens. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/
– Gill: Solomon knew the nature and uses of plants and animals. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-4.html

**v. 34** – Guzik: Solomon became famous even among kings (see notes on vv. 31–33). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-4/
– A short devotional note on Bible Hub's v. 29 page says people came from everywhere to hear him. It adds that all the knowledge needed for salvation is in Scripture. I couldn't confirm who wrote it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/4-29.htm
